Ferret
fĕr'ət
n. (a creeping thing of the unclean list; probably a gecko or a small burrowing animal)
Old French furet, from Latin fur, a thief — the little thief. The Hebrew anaqah is from a root meaning to cry out or groan, so the creature is named for a sound rather than a shape; many identify it with the gecko.

Biblical Definition

The word occurs once, first in the list of Leviticus 11:30: “And the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard, and the snail, and the mole.” It belongs with the seven other creatures of verses twenty-nine and thirty, all of them “unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth” (Lev 11:29). The rule attached is not about eating only: “whosoever doth touch them, when they be dead, shall be unclean until the even” (Lev 11:31). Anyone who has kept a house in a hot country knows why the list is full of the creatures that get into houses. And the chapter closes with the reason for the whole catalogue, which is not hygiene and not zoology: “For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy” (Lev 11:44). Peter quotes that verse to Christians who eat what they like, which is the clearest statement in the New Testament of what these chapters were always for.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the ferret as an animal of the weasel kind, red-eyed and used to drive rabbits from their burrows; and, as a verb, to drive out of a lurking place.

expand to see more

FERRET, n. [Fr. furet; L. fur, a thief.] An animal of the genus Mustela, or weasel kind, with red eyes.

It is used in driving rabbits out of their holes.

The ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard. Lev. xi.

FERRET, v.t. To drive out of a lurking place, as a ferret does a rabbit.

Key Scripture

Lev 11:30 — "And the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard, and the snail, and the mole."

Lev 11:31 — "These are unclean to you among all that creep: whosoever doth touch them, when they be dead, shall be unclean until the even."

Lev 11:44 — "For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth."

Lev 11:29 — "These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind,"

Modern Corruption

The dietary law is explained as ancient public health, which is to answer a question Leviticus 11:44 has already answered in the opposite terms.

expand to see more

The hygienic theory of the clean and unclean laws is popular in both directions — sceptics use it to make the law merely primitive medicine, and defenders use it to make the Bible scientifically advanced. Leviticus itself gives a different reason, and gives it as the conclusion of the whole chapter: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy. The distinctions were a daily, tactile discipline in separation, worked into what a family could put on the table, so that a nation could not eat a meal without being reminded that it belonged to God and was not like the peoples around it. That is a theological purpose, not a medical one, and it explains features no hygiene theory can — why touching a dead one defiles until evening, why the same chapter regulates ovens and vessels, and why the whole system is later declared fulfilled rather than merely outgrown.

That last point is where Christians must be careful in both directions. The Lord Jesus declared all meats clean, Peter was told on the housetop not to call common what God had cleansed, and Paul writes that the kingdom of God is not meat and drink. The ceremonial distinctions are fulfilled in Christ and are not binding on the church; a believer who reimposes them has, Colossians says, submitted to ordinances after the commandments and doctrines of men. But the purpose behind them is not abolished, because Peter quotes Leviticus 11:44 to Gentile churches: be ye holy; for I am holy. The separation moved from the plate to the life. What was once taught by a list of creatures is now taught by conduct, speech, and the ordering of a household — and the God who required it has not changed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew anaqah (H604), rendered ferret; from a root meaning to groan or cry out; with sheqets (H8263), a detestable thing, and qadash (H6942), to sanctify.

expand to see more

Hebrew anaqah (H604) — rendered ferret; from anaq, to cry out, so named from its sound; Leviticus 11:30.

Hebrew remes (H7431) — creeping things; the class to which the eight belong; Leviticus 11:29.

Hebrew tame (H2931) — unclean; the verdict on the whole list; Leviticus 11:31.

Hebrew qadash (H6942) — to sanctify, to set apart; ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves; Leviticus 11:44.

Greek hagios (G40) — holy; be ye holy; for I am holy, quoted to the churches; 1 Peter 1:16.

Usage

"“And the ferret, and the chameleon, and the lizard” — the creatures that get into houses."

"“Whosoever doth touch them, when they be dead, shall be unclean until the even” — a daily discipline."

"“Ye shall be holy; for I am holy” — the stated reason for the whole chapter."
